reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / KDIGO
clinicalPearls: A histological pattern rather than a single disease, defined by mesangial proliferation, thickened capillary walls, and a characteristic double-contour ('tram-track') appearance of the basement membrane
Modern classification is based on immunofluorescence, dividing it into immunoglobulin/immune-complex-mediated disease and complement-mediated C3 glomerulopathy
Immune-complex MPGN is driven by chronic antigenaemia, such as hepatitis C (often with cryoglobulins), chronic infections, autoimmune disease, or monoclonal gammopathy
Complement-mediated forms reflect dysregulation of the alternative pathway and overlap with C3 glomerulopathy
Presentations range from asymptomatic urinary abnormalities to nephrotic syndrome, nephritic features, or a mixed nephritic-nephrotic picture, often with low serum complement
Because it is a pattern of injury, the essential step is a thorough search for the underlying cause
Treatment is directed at the underlying driver, for example antiviral therapy for hepatitis C or addressing a monoclonal clone, alongside supportive renal care
Prognosis and specific therapy differ substantially between the immune-complex and complement-mediated subtypes
reference.pathophysiology: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis describes a pattern of glomerular injury in which deposits accumulate in the mesangium and subendothelial space, prompting mesangial cell proliferation and interposition into the capillary wall. This remodelling produces basement membrane duplication (double contours) and capillary wall thickening. The deposits may consist of immune complexes formed against persistent antigens (chronic infection, autoimmune disease, or monoclonal immunoglobulin) in immune-complex MPGN, or of complement components in complement-mediated disease due to alternative pathway dysregulation. Both routes activate complement and inflammatory cascades, resulting in proteinuria, haematuria, and progressive nephron loss.
additionalDifferentials: C3 glomerulopathy (as a related complement-mediated entity)
Chronic thrombotic microangiopathy (which can mimic the pattern)
additionalInvestigations: Serum complement (C3, C4) to help separate immune-complex from complement-mediated disease
Hepatitis B and C serology and cryoglobulin testing
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with free light chains
Autoimmune serology (e.g. ANA) where clinically indicated
Kidney biopsy with immunofluorescence and electron microscopy to subclassify
redFlags: Nephrotic-range proteinuria with falling kidney function
Systemic features of cryoglobulinaemia or vasculitis
Findings suggesting an occult malignancy or monoclonal process
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on the underlying cause and subtype; treating a reversible driver such as hepatitis C can improve outcomes, whereas complement-mediated and idiopathic forms often progress to kidney failure over years.
pitfalls: Treating the biopsy pattern without identifying and addressing the underlying cause
Failing to test for hepatitis C, cryoglobulins, or a monoclonal gammopathy
Not using immunofluorescence to distinguish immune-complex from C3-dominant disease
Assuming a uniform prognosis across all MPGN subtypes
